skyline.text: Nature gives you knobs and nurture turns them, says Amit Varma
How centuries of deep-sea diving reshaped a Korean island’s women
Why Darwin left William Paley’s designer out of a job

footnote.text: That is natural selection. There’s nothing more, nothing less.

brief.head: Levels of the pencil
brief.text: Level two sees a pencil’s complexity and calls for a central committee, Ajay Shah said. The highest level knows a self-organising system makes pencils out of thin air. {125-C02}

brief.head: Genes for hockey?
brief.text: Nature and nurture are correlated, Ajay Shah said. A hockey family passes on genes for explosive strength and early coaching, so we overstate what nature alone hands down. {125-C06}

brief.head: The boss is no tiger
brief.text: A charging lion wired us for instant fight or flight. A bad email from the boss, Ajay Shah said, can wait two hours for a reply. {125-C07}

brief.head: The laddoo test
brief.text: Evolution explains why a sweet tooth was selected long ago, not what you feel today, Amit Varma said. Nobody eating a laddoo thinks of calorie scarcity. {125-C08}

brief.head: Newton’s way out
brief.text: Newton reconciled science and faith, Ajay Shah said: God made laws like gravity, set the system going and let it whirl along. Biology allows the same move. {125-S03}

thought.text: A description of something doesn’t imply a prescription of anything.
thought.who: Amit Varma, warning against reading a morality into nature

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the forces that made us
lead.head: Know thyself, meet thy genes
body: Know thyself, urged the philosophers of ancient Greece. One way to do it, Amit Varma said, is to understand your hardwiring: the way evolution shaped you, and the separate way culture shaped you. {#knowthyself}

Ajay Shah’s turning point came as an economics PhD student, when he read Paul Ewald’s article on the evolution of virulence in *Scientific American*. “It just blew my mind and it was just a moment that you can’t unsee,” he said. {125-S02}

Varma came to it later, through Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*: the second great intellectual awakening of his life, after markets. Both, he said, share a bottom-up process of spontaneous order, with “no central planner, no grand designer”. {125-S01}
## Six statements
Before the biology, Varma cleared away misconceptions with five statements, then added a sixth.

The first was that natural selection is independent of God. William Paley saw in a watch on a beach, and in the human eye, the hand of a designer. “Darwin made the existence of a metaphorical watchmaker irrelevant,” Varma said. {125-C03}
Nor does nature settle what is good. Deriving an ought from an is, or equating the natural with the good, is a fallacy, Varma argued, on the right and the left alike.
Nature and nurture are not a binary either. In a line Varma attributes to Steven Pinker, nature gives you knobs, and nurture turns them. {125-C05}
His last warnings were about language and purpose. Genes want nothing, and evolution aims at nothing. “There is no mother evolution,” Shah said.
## Copies and competition

The mechanism itself is bare, Shah said: things that copy themselves, variation among them, and finite resources to fight over. The traits that win are refined, generation after generation, with no apex and no endpoint. {125-C10}

Sex shuffles genes and multiplies the variation selection works on, and mate choice adds a second engine. The two can clash: the springbok’s high leap impresses mates, but the lion simply waits for it to land. {125-C11}

Environment acts through gene expression. Children starved in the womb during the 1944 famine in Amsterdam grew up more prone to obesity, Shah said. Their DNA was unchanged, Varma stressed, so this was epigenetics, not Lamarckism. {125-C12}
Then came the examples, which Shah called wild: sickle cell and malaria, milk-drinking adults, Korea’s diving women, Britain’s blackened moths and cholera in the two Bengals.
## In no hurry
The unit of evolutionary time, Shah said, is the generation. {125-C14} Humans manage one every 25 years, about 400 in 10,000 years, so we are mostly the humans of 10,000 years ago.
Modernity, on that clock, has barely begun. “It was only the day before yesterday that the Magna Carta happened,” he said. {125-J19}

Varma’s final point was that the brain is part of the body, shaped by selection like every other organ, so some differences between men and women are hardwired. Admitting that, he insisted, does not justify treating anyone unequally. {125-C15}
That argument continues in a second part, built around Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam’s *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, which Varma calls a masterpiece.

Shah closed with a moral. Marvel at the eagle’s eye and resist the engineer’s urge to design one, he said: “this magic is made by an uncontrolled self-organizing system without any designer.” {125-C01}
Varma had the last word: “The only kind of eye I don’t like, Ajay, is the I in ego.” {125-J13}

second.label: Malaria’s bargain
second.head: The lion or the mosquito
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why a disorder that fells runners has survived
body: Sickle cell anaemia looks like a cruel flaw. Push the heart hard, Ajay Shah said, and red blood cells collapse into a sickle shape, so a person running from a leopard can crash to the ground. Why had such a trait not died out?
The answer is malaria. {125-S07} Its plasmodium hides inside red blood cells, out of reach of the immune system, and multiplies there. {#plasmodium} A sickled cell makes its life much harder.

Evolution struck a balance between peak cardiac capability and surviving malaria, Shah said, which is why entire communities in India carry sickle cell and thalassaemia. Amit Varma proposed a title for the short story: “The Lion and the Mosquito.” Shah corrected him: “The Lion or the Mosquito.” {125-J08}

quote.text: It turns out that thalassemia and sickle cell anemia are selected for in environments with malaria.

second.caption: sickle cell and malaria

third.head: Black is the new white
body: British moths were once white or off-white, Ajay Shah said. Then the industrial revolution brought poor-quality coal furnaces, their soot settled on buildings, and the walls turned black.

A white moth on a black wall was easy prey for birds. Darker moths survived better, and “within a couple of decades the moths of industrial revolution England turned black.” The example played a big role in the earliest debates over evolution. {125-S10}
Amit Varma spelt out the mechanism. Every generation throws up a few random dark mutants, and the environment decides which survive. {#mutants}

The same process, he said, breeds mosquitoes that resist insecticides and bacteria that resist antibiotics. Even if only 0.5 per cent of mosquitoes resist a treatment, those are the ones that survive and breed. {#halfpercent}
third.caption: the moths of industrial England

p2.title: How we were made
p2.deck: From God and the watchmaker to the brain, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah lay out natural selection

sections.label: Starting points
sections.head: Watch, but no watchmaker
sections.caption: God, Paley and the watchmaker
body: Before any biology, Amit Varma set out statements to clear away misconceptions. The first: natural selection is independent of God and of morality.

William Paley argued that a watch found on a beach, unlike a stone, must have a maker, and that the intricate human eye must likewise have a designer: God. Natural selection showed that random accidents of nature could build such intricacy from the bottom up. {125-C03}
That does not rule God out, Varma said. A believer can say God is so cool that he created the process called natural selection.

Ajay Shah offered Newton’s reconciliation: God made the laws, set the system going and let it whirl along. Biology allows the same move, he said, placing God at the first self-replicating molecules, or at the Big Bang. {125-S03}
## Is does not make ought

The second statement warned against David Hume’s is-ought fallacy, which derives a prescription from a description, and G. E. Moore’s naturalistic fallacy, which defines the good as the natural. {#hume}
Bigots once called homosexuality unnatural and so wrong, Varma said: a fallacy, and false besides. He faults Jordan Peterson on gender roles, and the left for denying differences between the sexes.

~ With what Adam Smith called the man of system, these fallacies fed early-20th-century eugenics on the left as well as the right, Varma said: H. G. Wells and George Bernard Shaw believed in it too. {125-J16}

quote.text: God made the laws. And He got a system going, and then the system whirled along.

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Wired one way, raised another
sections.caption: nature’s knobs
body: Nature and nurture are not a binary, Amit Varma said. He likes a line he is “pretty sure” is Steven Pinker’s, though neither he nor AI has found its source. {125-C05}

We are hardwired differently, he explained. Someone predisposed to anger can stay calm in a peaceful life. A placid person can lose his cool in a nasty, brutish one, or, Varma offered, if he keeps meeting Bengali economists. {125-J03}
Culture’s role, he argued, is to mitigate or amplify that hardware according to values we arrive at by thinking. That, to him, is the whole Enlightenment project.
## Old wiring, new world

Ajay Shah listed the old wiring: a craving for fat and sugar from times of scarce food, a hair-trigger fight-or-flight response, and tribalism from bands with a median size of 150 people. {#tribe} Culture is the operating system on top.
Shah also warned that we overstate nature. Talent seems to run in families partly because families pass on coaching and encouragement along with genes. {125-C06}

~ Varma added that social media companies chasing engagement have accidentally amplified our tribal instincts. As the rain poured down, he said, it was up to us to remember that the rain too will stop.

quote.text: Nature gives you knobs, nurture turns them.

sections.label: The mechanics
sections.head: Copy, vary, compete, repeat
sections.caption: the bare mechanics of selection
body: Natural selection needs little, Ajay Shah said. There must be things that make copies of themselves, organisms or even firms. {#copies} Their traits must vary. And resources must be finite, so they compete.
Better users of resources leave more copies, so their traits spread and, generation after generation, are refined “to fiendish levels of excellence”. There is no equality in it, and no end.
Amit Varma illustrated it with taste. Among fruit and poisonous plants, a mutation for liking bitter things could kill its carrier, so the sweet tooth and the aversion to bitterness spread. {#bitter}

Culture shapes taste too, within limits. He read out Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam: “We can learn to appreciate food that is bitter, like coffee or olives, but no culture enjoys cinnamon sprinkled feces.” {125-J18}
## The second engine

Sex, some three billion years ago, was an incredible innovation, Shah said: it shuffles genes and multiplies variation. {#threebillion} In complex creatures, mate choice adds a second engine, sexual selection.
~ The engines can pull apart. A springbok leaps high when chased, signalling health to mates, while the lion waits for it to land. Varma called it “a race to the top”. {125-J06}

quote.text: Evolution never ends. There is no apex outcome, there is no destination.

sections.label: Epigenetics
sections.head: The famine’s long shadow
sections.caption: the Amsterdam famine
body: If every human cell holds fixed DNA, two billion letters of it at birth, Ajay Shah asked, is everything about us programmed? {#twobillion}
No. Epigenetics, he said, studies gene expression: the way the environment interacts with the code written in DNA to produce different outcomes.
One of its most famous studies concerns Amsterdam in 1944. After a rebellion, the Nazis cut off the roads to starve the city. The Allies airdropped food, but a terrible famine followed.

Years later, scientists studied children exposed to the famine between conception and birth. Those starved in the womb had a much greater propensity to obesity, hoarding food more desperately, and the effect lasted several generations. {125-S13}
## Not Lamarck’s way

That sounds weirdly Lamarckian, Shah conceded. Amit Varma drew the line. Lamarckism holds that changes made in your lifetime, like a blacksmith’s strong arms, pass on through your genes. It was a common belief in the 19th century, and there is nothing to it. {125-S04}
~ The famine changed no one’s DNA, Varma said. It turned the sweetness knob up full, and the children ended up eating “a lot of laddoos, if laddoos were ever in Amsterdam”. {125-J07}

quote.text: Epigenetics did not change the DNA of the kids who were born at that time. It merely turned the knobs differently.

sections.label: Deep time
sections.head: The clock ticks in generations
sections.caption: evolution’s slow clock
body: Hearing that moths turned black in a few decades, people make a common mistake, Ajay Shah warned: the compression of time. {#compression}

Large mutations are generally a mistake, he said. Big changes are birth defects. Picture, he said, a complete mosquito with one tiny change: a little more ability to cope with DDT. The machine being modified is so complicated that too many changes at once make a mess. What works is a tiny change, accumulated over hundreds or thousands of generations.
That is how the eye was polished, including the eagle’s, which from two kilometres up can see a single mouse walking on the ground. {#eagle}
## Ten minutes or 25 years
Bacteria reproduce roughly every ten minutes, six generations an hour: a frightening pace that has made coping with them a major evolutionary force, shaping the human immune system. {#tenminutes}

Humans manage one generation every 25 years, Shah said: 400 in 10,000 years, which isn’t much. {#fourhundred} So we are mostly the humans of 10,000 years ago, and our hardware has not evolved for modern conditions.
~ Peace, civilisation and the rule of law are, by that measure, brand new. “The Magna Carta is 1215,” Shah said, “it’s like blink of an eye.” {125-J19}

quote.text: The unit of evolutionary timescale is not time, but generations

sections.label: The brain
sections.head: It doesn’t stop at the neck
sections.caption: the brain as part of the body
body: Amit Varma ended with a point he called almost obvious. Every cell of the body is designed by natural selection, so why imagine the brain is not? {125-C15}
No one denies that male and female bodies evolved differently, he said. Yet when it comes to the brain and behaviour, many people talk as if everything is culture.
Varma did not wave culture away. Society is patriarchal, he said, and cultures magnify some of the worst aspects of our nature. But many differences between men and women are also hardwired.
## Aware, not unequal
The task, he argued, is to be aware of those differences rather than deny them, and not to conclude that they require unequal treatment.

Ajay Shah had earlier made a related point: the voice in our heads is one evolutionary adaptation among many, and much of what drives us runs below awareness. There is complicated circuitry, he noted, that makes the heart beat. {#heartbeat}

~ The episode was groundwork. The hosts had meant to fold it into their episode on Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam’s *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, but split it in two, lest that become, in Varma’s words, “like a *Seen and the Unseen* eight-hour episode”. {125-J12}

quote.text: The brain is a part of the body, right? Every cell of our body is designed, as you pointed out, by natural selection, right?

side.boxText: Ghiselin, quoted by Amit Varma, said people could not handle the radical departure implicit in Darwin’s new cosmology: “A world in which the brain is itself an extension of the gonads simply cannot be reconciled with the old way of thinking.” {125-J15}

contQuote.text: Evolution is the ultimate success story of spontaneous order. That there is no central planner, there is no teleology, there is no objective, the system just keeps evolving on its own, and my God, it does amazing things.

p3.title: Selected stories
p3.deck: Diving women, milk drinkers and superbugs: evolution at work, and what it teaches

stories.start: And in my last example I want to go back right to the beginning
stories.end: then the incentives of the Covid change and the Covid becomes milder
stories.caption: cholera in the two Bengals
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how clean water tamed a killer
stories.head: A tale of two Bengals
body: In the early years after independence, Ajay Shah said, West Bengal improved its drinking water and cut its faecal contamination. In East Bengal, things stayed bad.

What followed was evolution at work. Where dirty water all but guaranteed that cholera reached new victims, it had no reason to keep its host alive. It killed fast, forcing the host into “crazy diarrhea” that infected the water supply.
In West Bengal, where transmission got harder, “the incentives of the cholera changed”, Shah said, crediting “the glories of the Republic of India”. Its strains evolved to be less virulent. {125-S12}

The idea comes from Paul Ewald, whose *Scientific American* article on the evolution of virulence hooked Shah on biology. A pathogen uses its host’s body to copy itself, then must jump to another host. Kill the host within a day or two, and it cannot get its copies out.

So a pathogen that passes feebly does best by keeping its host alive, while one that spreads easily can be rapacious. Depending on the complexity of transmission, Shah said, there is an optimal level of virulence. {125-C13}

He applied the logic to Covid. In a crowded Bombay suburban train or at the Maha Kumbh in Haridwar, the most rapacious strain wins. Masking and social distancing change the virus’s incentives, and it becomes milder.

~ Amit Varma, glad they had discussed semantics, reminded listeners that all of this is metaphor. Past pandemics, he noted, citing Chinmay Tumbe’s *The Age of Pandemics*, ended not because we eliminated the strain but because it evolved towards the least virulent. {125-R13}
stories.why: Public health does more than stop a disease spreading, Shah’s story suggests. By making transmission harder, clean water and masks change what a pathogen evolves into, and so can make the disease itself less deadly.
stories.postscript: Mid-explanation, Shah said of the pathogen, “Not that he’s thinking.” Varma: “Not that he’s a he.” {125-J10}

stories.start: The second example that I want to talk about is the ability
stories.end: the ability of some of us as adults to drink milk
stories.caption: the gene for drinking milk
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a mutation that built cattle cultures
stories.head: A mutation worth milking
body: All mammals make lactase as infants, to digest the lactose in milk, Ajay Shah said, and lose the ability as they grow up.
Then, maybe 7,000 or 8,000 years ago, on the border between Bulgaria and Turkey, a mutation let adults keep making it. {#lactase} The gene is called lactase persistence.

Milk became high-quality food for grown-ups, and whole cow-owning, cow-herding cultures grew around it. Its carriers reproduced well and conquered faraway lands, including northern India. The gene is still far more common in India’s north, where those invasions happened, than in its south. {125-S08}
~ Not everyone wins. Amit Varma spared a thought for the lactose-intolerant, who lack the gene but live in a culture that keeps asking them why they don’t drink milk.

quote.text: there was a mutation that was selected by natural selection and then the culture turned around and exploited that.

stories.start: My next example comes from Korea. There is a place, Amit, called Jeju Island.
stories.end: certain attributes being selected for in certain places before we are a globalized world
stories.caption: the divers of Jeju Island
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the deep-sea divers of Jeju Island
stories.head: Holding their breath for centuries
body: On Jeju Island in Korea, Ajay Shah said, women dive into the deep sea, for pearls as he put it, and diving has been the main livelihood for hundreds of years.

That set off natural selection. Women better able to hold their breath, process oxygen and cope with the pressure came back with the catch. Those less adapted tended to have accidents and die. Over hundreds of years, the divers developed remarkable physical adaptations. {125-S09}
It is a bit like the Sherpas of the high Himalayas, Shah said, with their unbelievable ability to cope with low oxygen.
~ Amit Varma added that the world’s top long-distance runners come from East Africa, where altitude, terrain and culture amplify the effect. {#runners}
stories.why: Natural selection is not only ancient history, the story shows. A livelihood that presses on a population steadily, generation after generation, can visibly reshape its biology, as the sea did on Jeju.

stories.start: But I mean as with uh mosquitoes and DDT I also want to say
stories.end: human uses of DDT or antibiotics and the process of how resistance develops
stories.caption: DDT and antibiotics
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on fogging, half-finished courses and resistance
stories.head: Half a dose, twice the trouble
body: When one housing colony does DDT fogging, Ajay Shah said, the neighbouring buildings get a partial dose. The mosquitoes that survive are those with a little resistance, and they breed the next generation. Do it at the scale of a population, he urged, not one colony at a time. {#fogging}

Antibiotics fail the same way. A full course drives a pathogen down so the immune system can finish it off. But people start feeling better within two or three weeks and stop, leaving the most resistant pathogens to surge back. {#course}
Each imperfect cycle breeds antimicrobial resistance. The individual feels fine, Shah said, “but at the level of a society, one by one we lose our silver bullets.” {125-S11}
~ Amit Varma summed it up: “Evolutionary theory meets human hubris.” {#hubris}
stories.why: A partial dose is worse than none, because it selects for resistance. Individual incentives, to fog one colony or stop a course on feeling better, wear down assets that belong to everyone, which is why Shah calls this a public health problem.

quiz.q: Why do sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia persist, though they can fell someone running hard?
quiz.a: They are selected for where malaria is common, making the plasmodium’s survival harder.

quiz.q: Asked by a reporter how to get another Kapil Dev, what did the cricketer reply?
quiz.a: That his father was dead and his mother was too old.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s father teach his children using Dara Singh’s strong daughter?
quiz.a: That strength came from genes and upbringing, not Dara Singh’s bodybuilding: not Lamarckism.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s pencil ladder, what does the person on level two conclude?
quiz.a: That anything so complex needs a central committee directing the aluminium and steel.

quiz.q: What, in Ajay Shah’s view, is the unit of evolutionary timescale?
quiz.a: Not time but generations: humans manage about 400 in 10,000 years.

quiz.q: What happened to Britain’s white moths when industrial soot blackened the buildings?
quiz.a: Birds picked them off, and within a couple of decades the moths turned black.
